card.thesis: This engine cannot express relative strength: entry and exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so there is no way to buy 'the strongest semiconductor name' or trade a spread. What this card actually does is apply one absolute condition -- close above its own 50-day average with RSI(14) between 55 and 80, i.e. a confirmed, non-extreme uptrend -- identically to a 9-name cyclical-semiconductor universe (NVDA AMD MU INTC MRVL AVGO TSM QCOM SOXX), and cap concurrent holdings at 3 of 9. That cap is the only 'rotation' logic available: the mechanism is that semiconductor demand and AI-capex cycles tend to move the whole group together and to persist for quarters rather than days, so entering only into names already confirmed in trend, and exiting on trend break or momentum fade, should keep capital on the right side of the cycle more often than not, while the cap prevents any single session from committing to more than 3 names at once. I measured pairwise daily-return correlation across these 9 names over the trailing ~253 sessions through 2026-02-13: mean 0.589, range 0.286 (INTC vs AVGO) to 0.824 (SOXX vs TSM). That is high -- this is a concentrated sector bet dressed as a 3-of-9 rotation, not a diversified basket, and I am not pretending otherwise. It is not a coin-flip between one name and nothing, though: breadth genuinely varies session to session under the proposed filter (median 4 of 9 names qualifying; at least 4 qualify on 50.6% of sessions, at least 6 on 21.3%), so the cap binds and actually forces a choice often enough to matter. When more than 3 names qualify on the same session, the broker fills entries in the fixed order the universe list is written -- alphabetical here -- not by any measure of relative strength, momentum magnitude, or liquidity. That is an arbitrary tiebreak, not a 'buy the leader' mechanism, and the card cannot do better than that. On the other side of these trades: momentum/trend traders who initiated the move earlier and are already positioned before this rule confirms it; mean-reversion sellers who fade strength too early inside a still-intact uptrend and get run over; and dip-buyers in choppy or declining regimes who buy bottoms this rule cannot see coming and will instead get chopped by.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and rsi(14) > 55 and rsi(14) < 80

card.thesis: Momentum exists because information diffuses and positions build slowly: institutional flows into a strengthening sector are staged over weeks (mandate reviews, index-fund rebalancing lags, analysts revising estimates in sequence rather than all at once), and short-horizon traders and dip-buyers who fade the first leg of a move get run over and forced to chase, extending it further. The people on the other side are the ones who sold or shorted the early leg on a mean-reversion prior and are still underwater when the second leg arrives. This is a diffusion-and-crowding story, not a single mispriced fact, which is why it decays slowly rather than being arbitraged away overnight. The entry requires three things at once: a short-term breakout (close crossing above its 20-day average), that breakout occurring above the 100-day average (a cheap, conventional context filter -- do not fight the intermediate trend), and RSI(14) above 55 confirming the move actually has thrust rather than being a one-bar wiggle. I measured this filter directly (see memo) and it is NOT a strong lever: it modestly cuts trade count in both chop windows (-8% in chop-2015, -4% in chop-2011) but its effect on average per-trade return is small and inconsistent, and in gfc it is measurably worse than the unfiltered rule on a per-trade basis. The real defense against chop in this design is the fast discretionary exit (price closing back below its own 20-day average), which keeps the average holding period to 6-13 sessions across every regime I measured, including both chop windows -- short enough that a whipsaw round-trip costs a small, bounded amount rather than compounding into a large loss. In both chop windows tested, zero trades reached the 8% stop within a 40-day hold; the stop is a tail backstop, not the routine risk control. I am not claiming this rule profits from chop -- it is roughly flat to modestly positive per trade in both chop windows, which is the honest finding: momentum does not get shredded here, but it does not have an edge here either, and the edge this rule has belongs to trending regimes.
card.entry: close crosses_above sma(20) and close > sma(100) and rsi(14) > 55

card.thesis: A 200-day moving average is a slow proxy for whether the marginal buyer still controls the tape. Structural forced sellers -- pensions and mandate-bound funds de-risking after a sustained decline, and levered holders forced out by drawdown -- keep supplying stock into a market that has been falling for months, which is exactly what 'price below its own 200-day average' detects; staying out during that condition avoids selling into their hands and re-enters only once buyers have re-established control on a monthly-to-quarterly timescale. Applying the same filter independently across four largely uncorrelated exposures (US equities SPY, international developed equities EFA, long Treasuries TLT, gold GLD) means one asset's trend break does not force the whole book to cash: in a rate-driven equity bear, the flight-to-quality bid that keeps bonds and gold trending up is a countercyclical buyer the strategy rides while equities are excluded, so exposure and return both keep coming from somewhere. Pre-registered failure regime: a sideways, choppy, low-trend market has no edge for this filter and pays repeated whipsaw entries/stop-outs against a benchmark that simply sits still; and a regime where every asset class de-rates together (a simultaneous equity-and-bond bear, e.g. a rate shock) removes nearly the whole book to cash-like exposure at once, leaving the strategy flat while a buy-and-hold benchmark may partially recover before the filter re-engages.

A directional move confirmed by both price above its 200-day average and the 50-day average itself above the 200-day tends to persist for months, not days: information about a regime change (a growth slowdown, a rate cycle turning, a flight to quality) diffuses slowly through institutional flows -- pension rebalancing, CTA and risk-parity positioning, 401k contribution timing -- that chase a confirmed trend rather than anticipate the turn. The counterparties who fund this are short-horizon mean-reversion and reversal traders who fade extended moves and value investors anchored to a stale price, both of whom get run over by continuation exactly when the trend has already cleared this rule's confirmation bar. The universe spans four macro-sensitive asset classes on purpose -- broad equity beta (SPY), growth beta (QQQ), a defensive equity proxy (XLU), duration (TLT) and a monetary hedge (GLD) -- so that when equities are trend-negative, capital has somewhere else in the same universe to be trend-positive: bonds and gold trending up specifically when equities trend down is a structural flight-to-quality correlation, not a coincidence, and it is what this card is actually betting on to avoid being flat-to-negative in every falling regime at once. I expect this to lose in bull-2024: a rule that requires both conditions to already be true cannot buy the first leg of a smooth, low-volatility rally, so it structurally captures less than its exposure-adjusted share of a market that never gives it a drawdown to sidestep, and it pays whipsaw costs getting positioned late.

Sector SPDRs oscillate around a short-term fair-value anchor because most of their daily volume comes from liquidity providers, index rebalancers and short-horizon momentum traders rather than investors repricing fundamentals -- fundamentals for a nine-sector basket do not change materially week to week. When RSI(14) drops below 30 AND the close is also below the 20-day, 2-stddev Bollinger lower band, two independent measures (momentum exhaustion and a statistically stretched price relative to recent volatility) agree that the move has overshot. The other side of that trade is forced or reflexive selling that does not price on fair value -- stop-loss cascades, volatility-targeting deleveraging, tax-loss and rebalancing flows -- and it does not persist once the flow clears, which is why we exit on the close reclaiming the 20-day mean rather than holding for a trend. This mechanism needs mean reversion to actually be the dominant force, which is true in a range-bound market and false in a fast one-directional break, where 'oversold' does not mean 'done falling' and the entry buys into a crash that keeps crashing. We measured this directly: in chop-2015 the rule produced 23 trades averaging +2.42% (70% win rate); in chop-2011, 25 trades averaging +0.93% (72% win rate). In covid the same rule, unchanged, produced 18 trades averaging -6.53% with a 17% win rate and 15 of 18 exits were stops -- see the memo for the full comparison and the sensitivity check confirming this split is not an artifact of the specific thresholds chosen.

The 200-day moving average is not a statistical artifact -- it is a level thousands of participants mechanically watch and react to at the same time (managed-futures CTAs, trend-following mutual funds, and technically-oriented traders all use variants of it), so a break of it triggers correlated follow-on flow rather than random noise. The other side of the trade is supplied by participants who are slow or unwilling to move: index funds and 401k flows that buy/sell on a schedule unrelated to price level, and holders exhibiting the disposition effect who keep underwater positions past the point a trend-follower would already have exited, cushioning the trend-follower's fills. Applying the identical rule independently across three assets whose price drivers are structurally different (US equity beta, long-duration interest-rate risk, and a non-yielding hard asset with its own supply/demand book) means the three trend signals are not forced to fire together -- when equity trend breaks down in a genuine flight-to-quality event, rate or gold trend can still be up, which a single-asset or single-sector trend book cannot offer. This is not a hedge (the rules do not compare symbols to each other -- the engine cannot do that); it is three independent bets whose bad years are not the same years, which the correlation numbers in the memo support. What I expect to go wrong: fast V-shaped shocks. A 200-day average reacts on the order of weeks, not days, so a crash-and-snapback that completes inside a single quarter (COVID is the designed example) will be entered late on the way down and re-entered late on the way back up, capturing the worst of both transitions rather than avoiding them.

card.display_name: Band Reversion — Broad Market & Sector ETFs
card.thesis: Mechanism: a close below the 20-day, 2-stdev Bollinger lower band while price still sits above its 200-day SMA is disproportionately forced, price-insensitive selling inside an intact uptrend -- stop-loss cascades from levered/margin accounts, mechanical VaR/vol-target de-risking by risk-parity and vol-targeting funds reacting to a spike in realised volatility, and index/ETF authorized-participant redemption flow. None of that flow carries a fundamental view; the 200-day trend filter is the proxy for 'nothing structural has changed yet'. The counterparty on my entry is that forced seller. Once the flow clears, price tends to revert toward the 20-day mean as valuation-insensitive rebalancers (funds trading back to target weight) and short-term dip buyers step back in; my exit sells into that reversion at the middle band, before it can be told apart from a genuine trend resumption. Pre-registered failure regime: a fast, deep, sustained decline where the 200-day SMA (which is slow by construction) has not yet turned down before the crash accelerates -- GFC's Sep-Oct 2008 leg and COVID's Feb-Mar 2020 leg are the two candidates. In that regime the entry keeps firing on 'dips' that are actually the first third of a much larger decline, the 20-day reversion does not arrive inside the 20-day hold, and positions exit on the stop or the time cap at a loss, repeatedly, until the 200-day SMA finally rolls over and the filter shuts the strategy off -- likely after most of the damage in that leg is already done.

In heavily-optioned, high-open-interest instruments (broad index ETFs and major sector SPDRs), a period of contracting realized volatility is systematically accompanied by net-short-gamma positioning among option sellers -- covered-call overlay funds, options-income strategies, and dealer desks that have sold volatility into the calm and hedge by trading against price. While the range holds, that flow is stabilizing: dealers buy dips and sell rips, compressing range further. When price finally closes outside the upper band while realized volatility (ATR-14) is still below its own longer-run baseline (ATR-50), the move has started before the option-selling crowd has repriced -- their short-gamma hedging flips from stabilizing to reinforcing (short calls forces the dealer/writer to buy into the breakout to stay hedged), mechanically extending the initial move for a period afterward. The other side of this trade is the option seller who wrote premium assuming continued range-bound behavior and is now a forced, mechanical buyer. What is expected to go wrong: this mechanism is about the first burst of a volatility regime change, not persistence. In a slow grinding bear (rate-driven, low realized-vol decline) there may be few or no valid low-ATR breakouts to trade, and the strategy should sit mostly in cash -- underperforming a benchmark that keeps drifting down slowly without ever tripping the squeeze condition. It is also vulnerable to a crash that gaps straight through the band with ATR already elevated (already-expanded, not compressed, volatility) -- COVID's opening days looked like that -- in which case the squeeze filter correctly refuses the entry, but a separate, unfiltered breakout would have caught the early down-move it is not designed to catch (this strategy is long-only).
card.entry: close crosses_above bb_upper(20,2.0) and atr(14) < atr(50)

card.thesis: A close that breaks above a confirmed multi-week swing high forces two groups to act, not just one: short sellers who sold into the old resistance are now underwater and mechanically buy to cover, and systematic trend/breakout funds (CTA-style N-day-high rules are a large, well-documented share of managed-futures and momentum flow) generate a fresh buy signal on the same event. Both are non-discretionary, price-triggered flows, which is why a break of an established range tends to keep going for a while rather than immediately mean-revert -- the buying is not opinion, it is a rule firing. The sma(200) trend filter restricts entries to sectors already in a primary uptrend, because a break of a local high inside a primary downtrend is disproportionately a bear-market rally, not a fresh trend. What I expect to go wrong: a grinding, broad-based bear (bear-2022-style) still produces some sector-level breakout signals -- sectors do not top in lockstep -- and those are precisely the trades that get overrun when the broader decline catches up, so I expect this card's worst window to be a bear regime, not a crash. See memo for the measured entry-frequency-by-window breakdown that grounds this.
card.entry: close crosses_above swing_high(20) and close > sma(200)

card.thesis: In a systemic equity selloff capital does not vanish, it rotates: institutional and retail sellers de-risk out of equities into US duration (Treasuries) and, in uncertainty-driven episodes, into gold. That rotation shows up first as a volatility breakout in the receiving instrument's own price -- a close pushing above its 20-day Bollinger upper band -- because a sudden, forced buying wave widens the band and breaks it before any slower moving-average filter would confirm a trend. The other side of that trade is whoever is still willing to sell duration or gold at the pre-rotation price: in ordinary markets TLT and GLD are unremarkable, low-conviction holdings that drift on yield and macro views with no connection to equity risk, so a band breakout in either is a cheap, low-information signal most of the time and costs a string of small whipsaw losses. It becomes a strong, well-paid signal exactly when equity holders are forced, non-price-sensitive sellers of risk and buyers of safety, because that is the one condition under which the other side of a TLT/GLD trade is not a considered view but a stampede. This card holds TLT and GLD outright -- real capital, real price risk, sized at 15% of starting equity per slot -- so its payoff comes from a position actually carried through the dislocation, not from sitting out of SPY while it falls; roughly 85% of the book is uninvested cash at any time, which this engine scores as free but which a real book would have to fund, invest, or forgo yield on. I expect this card's numerically worst window to be bull-2024: a strong, low-volatility equity year gives TLT and GLD no rotation to catch, so the entry still fires on ordinary volatility noise, whipsaws against sma(20), and pays its premium with nothing to show for it. Separately, and worth flagging even though it is not the predicted worst *number*: bear-2022 is the window where the underlying mechanism itself fails, not just goes unpaid -- 2022 was a rate-hike-driven decline that hurt equities and duration together, so there was no flight-to-quality rotation into TLT to catch, and the card's raw return there is a real loss (the low-exposure denominator in the scoring only cushions how that loss compares to the benchmark, it does not mean the trade worked).

A confirmed swing-high breakout marks the point where a market has absorbed all the supply that capped it at the old pivot -- the resting sellers at that level have been cleared, so the next marginal buyer transacts at a new equilibrium with less overhead resistance above. The counterparty giving up the trade is the anchoring seller who priced the old high as fair value and is now underwater on that anchor; they cover or step aside rather than average down into a level that just failed to hold. This mechanism is not equity-specific -- it is a statement about order-book supply and anchoring bias, so it should recur in any liquid, exchange-traded, trend-capable market: government bonds, gold, investment-grade credit, not just stock indices. Round 1's breakout card tested that claim with nine US sector ETFs, which are nine expressions of the same equity-beta trend and were later measured near 0.58 mean pairwise correlation -- one bet in nine costumes, which is why its win rate moved by window and not by symbol within a window. This card tests the mechanism across four assets chosen specifically because their return drivers differ (equity risk premium, interest-rate duration, monetary/safe-haven demand, investment-grade credit spread), and reports the measured correlation matrix rather than asserting diversification. The trend filter (price above its 200-day average) is there to avoid buying a breakout that is really a dead-cat bounce inside a larger downtrend; it also means the strategy is structurally absent during the worst of a fast crash, which is arithmetic, not risk management, and is declared as such rather than claimed as skill.
card.entry: close crosses_above swing_high(20) and close > sma(200)
